title: From tree to notebook
text:
Every page in your notebook began as a tree, or sometimes as an older notebook. Paper-makers all over the world follow almost the same steps.

First, tree trunks are cut into short logs and the bark is peeled away. Many paper companies grow their own trees on large plantations and plant new ones to replace those that they cut down. The bark is useful too, because it can be burned to make heat for the factory.

Next, the logs are chopped into small chips. The chips are cooked in a huge tank with water and chemicals, which dissolve the sticky glue that holds the wood together. What remains is a soft, wet mass of tiny fibres called pulp. Pulp is then washed many times and, if the paper is meant to be white, it is bleached.

The pulp is mixed with a great deal of water until it looks like thin, milky soup. It is sprayed onto a moving screen. The water drains through the screen, and the fibres are left behind, tangled together in a thin, wet sheet. This tangling is what makes paper strong.

After that, the wet sheet travels between heavy rollers that squeeze out most of the remaining water. Then it passes over hot metal cylinders that dry it completely. At the end of the machine, the paper is wound onto an enormous roll as wide as a classroom.

Finally, the roll is cut into sheets, which are packed, sent to a printer and bound into notebooks.

Recycled paper starts at a different point. Used paper is collected, sorted and mixed with water to make pulp, so no new trees are needed for that part of the process. Paper fibres can be recycled several times, but they become shorter and weaker each time. This is why recycled paper often feels rougher than new paper.
